sections.normalized_html:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, the larger cone ([MATH: Q]) is similar to the smaller one ([MATH: P]) with a scale factor of [MATH: k = \dfrac{9\,\textrm{in}}{6\,\textrm{in}} = \dfrac{3}{2}.]

Thus, the ratio of the volume is [MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac32\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{8},] and we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = \dfrac{27}{8}.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 56\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get [MATH: V_{Q}|= (27)/(8) ⋅ V_{P}; = (27)/(8) ⋅ 56; = 189in^{3}.]

The surface area of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 36\,\textrm{in}^2,] and the surface area of prism [MATH: Q] is [MATH: 324\,\textrm{in}^2.] If the volume of prism [MATH: P] is [MATH: 50\,\textrm{in}^3,] what is the volume of prism [MATH: Q?]

sections.normalized_html:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then

  • the ratio of the corresponding surface areas equals [MATH: k^2,] and

  • the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, prism [MATH: Q] is larger than prism [MATH: P.] Computing the ratio of the surface areas, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{A}_Q}{\mathcal{A}_P} = \dfrac{324\,\textrm{in}^2}{36\,\textrm{in}^2} = 9.]

This means that the solids are similar with a scale factor of [MATH: k = \sqrt{9} = 3.]

Thus, the ratio of the volumes is [MATH: k^3 = 3^3 = 27,] and we have [MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = 27.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting in [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 50\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get [MATH: V_{Q}|= 27 ⋅ V_{P}; = 27 ⋅ 50in^{3}; = 1,350in^{3}.]

items.title: Finding the Volume of a Combined Solid

sections.normalized_html: Two similar toy packaging boxes, [MATH: U] and [MATH: W,] are in the shape of right rectangular prisms. The surface area of box [MATH: U] is [MATH: 25~\mathrm{in}^2,] and the surface area of box [MATH: W] is [MATH: 49~\mathrm{in}^2.] The volume of box [MATH: W] is [MATH: 686~\mathrm{in}^3.] What is the total volume, in cubic inches [MATH: (\mathrm{in}^3),] of both boxes?
sections.readable_text: Two similar toy packaging boxes, [MATH: U] and [MATH: W,] are in the shape of right rectangular prisms. The surface area of box [MATH: U] is [MATH: 25~\mathrm{in}^2,] and the surface area of box [MATH: W] is [MATH: 49~\mathrm{in}^2.] The volume of box [MATH: W] is [MATH: 686~\mathrm{in}^3.] What is the total volume, in cubic inches [MATH: (\mathrm{in}^3),] of both boxes?

sections.normalized_html:
First, let’s introduce our notation:

  • Let [MATH: k] be the scale factor of similarity between the two boxes.

  • Let [MATH: S_U = 25] and [MATH: S_W = 49] represent the surface areas of boxes [MATH: U] and [MATH: W,] respectively.

  • Let [MATH: V_U] and [MATH: V_W = 686] represent the volumes of boxes [MATH: U] and [MATH: W,] respectively.

Since the ratio of surface areas equals the square of the scale factor, we have [MATH: k|= sqrt((S_{U})/(S_{W})); = sqrt((25)/(49)); = (5)/(7).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we'll practice spotting scale factors of three-dimensional shapes and converting cleanly between length, area, and volume proportionality coefficients.

---

Item 2 — Example: Working From Length to Surface Area or Volume in Similar Solids

Example Prompt:
Cone [MATH: P] has a height of [MATH: 6\,\textrm{in}] and is similar to cone [MATH: Q,] which has a height of [MATH: 9\,\textrm{in}.] The volume of cone [MATH: P] is [MATH: 56\,\textrm{in}^3.] What is the volume of cone [MATH: Q?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding volumes equals [MATH: k^3.]

Here, the larger cone ([MATH: Q]) is similar to the smaller one ([MATH: P]) with a scale factor of
[MATH: k = \dfrac{9\,\textrm{in}}{6\,\textrm{in}} = \dfrac{3}{2}.]

Thus, the ratio of the volume is [MATH: k^3 = \left(\dfrac32\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{8},] and we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathcal{V}_Q}{\mathcal{V}_P} = \dfrac{27}{8}.]

Solving for [MATH: \mathcal{V}_Q] and substituting [MATH: \mathcal{V}_P = 56\,\textrm{in}^3,] we get
[MATH: V_{Q}|= (27)/(8) ⋅ V_{P}; = (27)/(8) ⋅ 56; = 189in^{3}.]

If two solids are similar with scale factor [MATH: k,] then the ratio of the corresponding surface areas equals [MATH: k^2.]
